 Judgment

This Criminal Appeal is preferred by the appellant/accused under Section 374(3) of Cr.P.C.,
assailing the judgment of conviction and order of sentence dated 01.06.2023 passed in C.C.
No.16181/2020 by the XVI Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Bengaluru, whereby the appellant was convicted for the offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs.6,00,000/-, in default to undergo simple imprisonment for one year, out of which Rs.5,90,000/- was directed to be paid to the complainant as compensation under Section 357 of Cr.P.C.
2.

entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and conviction, the accused has preferred the present appeal under Sec.374(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 seeking to set aside the same.
3. The accused in CC No.16181/2020 before the trial court has preferred the instant appeal against the complainant.

The appellant and respondent are hereby assigned with their original ranks before the trial court i.e., the appellant as accused and respondent as complainant in CC No.16181/2020 in the instant discussion for the purpose of brevity and convenience to avoid the confusion and perplexity.

4. The respondent/complainant initiated private complaint under Section 200 Cr.P.C. alleging that the appellant, who was known to her for several years as a family friend, had approached her in the last week of January 2017 seeking financial assistance for improvement of his business.
5. It was her case that on 01.02.2017, she and her husband advanced a total sum of Rs.5,00,000/- to the accused, comprising Rs.3,00,000/- by RTGS and Rs.2,00,000/- by cash.
The accused allegedly promised to repay the same within two years.

6. Upon demand after expiry of the agreed period, the accused issued cheque bearing No.663709 dated 13.08.2020 for Rs.5,00,000/- drawn on State Bank of Mysuru, T. Narasipura Branch, towards discharge of the said liability.
7. The cheque, when presented through Karnataka Bank Ltd., Uttarahalli Branch, was dishonoured on 17.08.2020 for "Funds Insufficient".
Statutory notice dated 28.08.2020 was issued and served.

Though reply was sent, the amount was not paid, resulting in filing of complaint on 28.09.2020.
8.
The Trial Court, after recording sworn statement and marking Ex.P1 to Ex.P13, took cognizance and secured the presence of the accused.
The accused pleaded not guilty.
9. The complainant examined herself as PW-1 and produced documentary evidence.

The Srinivas vs M B Chandrakumari on 4 April, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/194172112/
2
cross-examination of PW-1 was partly conducted; however, the accused remained absent thereafter.
Further cross-examination was taken as nil.
The accused did not enter the witness box, nor adduce defence evidence.

10. The Trial Court, invoking the summary nature of proceedings under Section 143 of the Negotiable Instruments Act and relying on the directions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Indian Bank Association v. Union of India, proceeded to decide the matter on merits and convicted the accused.

entities.text: Indian Bank Association v. Union of India
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
11. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment passed by the trial court, the appellant being accused before the trial court has preferred the instant appeal against the respondent who was the complainant before the trial court on the following:
GROUNDS OF APPLEAL a) The appellant submits to the kind attention of this Hon'ble Court that the above said judgment is not in accordance with law, is not sustainable and is contrary to the evidence and materials available in the case.
b) The Trial Court has failed to exercise its jurisdiction in a proper manner.

c) The appellant submits that the Trial Court, without noticing the contradictions and deficiencies in the evidence given by the respondent and in the documents on record,
has given unnecessary importance only to the evidence of the respondent, thereby causing injustice to the appellant in the judgment.
d) Though the evidence available in this case is not supportive of the respondent's case, the Trial Court has failed to extend the benefit of doubt to this appellant.

e) On perusal of the entire facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence of the respondent, it is clear that there was no legally enforceable liability between the appellant and the respondent.
The respondent has also failed to prove the same.
However, the Trial Court has ignored these vital aspects/issues.
f) In this case, the Trial Court had posted the matter on 11-01-2023 for cross- examination of the respondent.

On that day, in the absence of the accused/appellant, the counsel for the accused/appellant sought time for cross- examination, and the Trial Court granted final opportunity and posted the matter to 17-02-2023.
On that day also, the counsel for the accused/appellant sought time and the Court granted time till 21-03-2023 subject to payment of Rs.500/- costs in the presence of the accused/appellant.

Thereafter, on 21-03-2023, in the absence of the accused/appellant, the cross- examination of the respondent was conducted and for further cross- Srinivas vs M B Chandrakumari on 4 April, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/194172112/
3
examination time was sought, and the Trial Court posted the matter to 20-04- 2023.

On that day, as the accused/appellant and his counsel were absent, the case was called at 12:20 PM and the Court considered that there was no further cross-examination on behalf of the accused/appellant and issued Non- Bailable Warrant against the accused/appellant.
The Trial Court failed to grant opportunity for further cross- examination and the counsel also failed to inform the appellant about the above said proceedings.
g) In this case, the Trial Court has not issued any notice or proclamation to the appellant and even the counsel for the appellant has not informed him about the proceedings before the Trial Court.
h) In this case, during cross-examination, the respondent has stated in the chief examination affidavit that the appellant approached in January 2018 seeking loan.
She has admitted that before and after the alleged disputed transaction, there was no monetary transaction between her and the accused.

Though she admitted that she had given Rs.2,00,000/- to the appellant in January 2017,
she has not stated on which date the appellant requested money and on which date she paid the amount.
The Trial Court has failed to judicially appreciate these admissions made in cross-examination.
I) In this case, regarding the disputed cheque, the respondent has stated in cross- examination that "I have enquired about the validity of cheque marked as Ex.P1.
I am aware that SBM Bank was merged with SBI Bank in 2017."
However, the respondent has not produced any document before the Trial Court to show that the cheque of the appellant was a valid cheque.
The Trial Court has failed to judicially consider these aspects.
j) In this case, the appellant suffered severe paralysis in the month of May 2023 and was taking treatment from traditional doctors for more than one year.
Therefore, he was not in a position to give proper instructions to his counsel and to lead defence evidence and mark documents.

l) In this case, the respondent has nowhere stated in her cross-examination that she paid Rs.5,00,000/- to the appellant and she has not produced any documents before the Trial Court to show that she was financially capable of lending such amount to the appellant.
The Trial Court has failed to judicially appreciate these aspects.

m) In this case, the Trial Court has committed error by not properly examining and verifying the authorship of the writing in Ex.P1, and without proper scrutiny and evaluation of evidence, has discussed irrelevant aspects and passed the impugned order contrary to law.
n) From the evidence of the respondent and the documents produced, it is clear that the cheque in question was issued only as security.

Srinivas vs M B Chandrakumari on 4 April, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/194172112/
4 o)
In the impugned judgment of the lower Court, grave injustice has been caused to this appellant.
p) If the impugned judgment and order of the lower Court is not set aside and if it remains as final order, the appellant will suffer irreparable loss permanently.

On these and other allied grounds, the appellant/accused pray before this court to call for entire records from the trial court, set aside the impugned judgment conviction and sentence passed by Trial Court in CC No.16181/2020 dated 01.06.2023 and acquit the accused from the alleged offence by allowing this appeal in the interest of justice and equity.

12. On the basis of the materials available on record following points arise for my consideration:
1) Whether the appellant has made out grounds to Condone the delay of 371 days in preferring the present appeal?
2) Whether the Trial Court has committed any illegality or perversity in holding that the cheque in question was issued towards discharge of legally enforceable debt and that the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is proved?
3) Whether the appellant was denied fair and reasonable opportunity to defend the case?
 4) Whether the impugned judgment  of conviction and sentence  warrants interference?
 5) What order?
13.

My findings to the above points are as under:
Point No.1: In the Affirmative Point No.2: In the Negative Point No.3: In the Negative Point No.4: In the Negative Point No.5: As per final order for the following:

REASONS 14. Point No.1:- The delay in preferring the present appeal is of 371 days, and the appellant has filed a separate application supported by a sworn affidavit explaining the circumstances under which the delay has occurred.

It is specifically averred that the appellant had suffered severe paralysis and he had taken traditional Ayurvedic treatment for more than one year and therefore, he could not render instructions to his advocate for filing appeal in time.
By the time, he would do so, there was delay of 371 days.
The delay was not intentional but for the bona-fide reasons stated above.

The explanation, on its face, does not disclose any deliberate inaction, willful negligence or mala fide design, but rather reflects procedural lapses and professional communication gaps which are humanly possible in the ordinary course of litigation.

15. It is now well settled that the expression "sufficient cause" occurring in Section 5 of the Limitation Act must receive a liberal and justice-oriented construction so as to advance substantial Srinivas vs M B Chandrakumari on 4 April, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/194172112/
5 justice rather than defeat it on technical grounds.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag v. Mst. Katiji, (1987) 2 SCC 107, has authoritatively held that refusal to condone delay results in a meritorious matter being thrown out at the very threshold and that courts must adopt a pragmatic and liberal approach while considering applications for condonation of delay.

entities.text: Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag v. Mst. Katiji, (1987) 2 SCC 107
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The delay in the present case though inordinate, however, the explanation tendered appears natural and plausible, especially in the context of criminal proceedings where the right to appeal is a substantive statutory safeguard.

16. Viewed in the cumulative backdrop of the explanation offered, the length of delay, and the absence of any discernible mala-fides, this Court is of the considered view that the appellant has shown "sufficient cause" within the meaning of Section 5 of the Limitation Act.
Denial of condonation in such circumstances would amount to foreclosing the appellant's statutory right of appeal on hyper-technical grounds.
Accordingly, the delay of 371 days deserves to be condoned in the interest of justice.
Hence, the Point No.1 is answered in the Affirmative.
17. Point No.2 to 4:-
18. The offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is a statutory offence incorporating reverse onus.
Once execution of cheque is admitted or proved, the Court is bound to raise presumptions under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the Act.
19. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rangappa v. Sri Mohan authoritatively held that the presumption under Section 139 includes presumption of existence of legally enforceable debt or liability.

20. Similarly, in Kumar Exports v. Sharma Carpets, it was held that the accused must raise a probable defence either through cross-examination or by leading evidence to rebut the statutory presumption.
In the case on hand, the accused did not dispute signature on the cheque.
He did not deny relationship.
In reply notice, he admitted borrowing Rs.3,00,000/-.
Thus, foundational facts stood established.

Srinivas vs M B Chandrakumari on 4 April, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/194172112/
6 21.
The cheque dated 13.08.2020 was presented within validity period.
Dishonour memo dated 17.08.2020 is supported by statutory presumption under Section 146 of the Act.
22. Legal notice dated 28.08.2020 was issued within 30 days and complaint was filed within limitation.

Therefore, the complainant complied with all mandatory requirements under Section 138.
23.
The appellant contends that the cheque was issued as security.

It is now settled that even a security cheque, if presented towards legally enforceable liability, attracts Section 138.
24.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar has held that even blank signed cheque voluntarily handed over attracts presumption and liability unless rebutted.
25. The accused neither entered the witness box nor elicited material admissions in cross-examination to probabilise the defence of security cheque.
Mere suggestion in reply notice is insufficient.
26. The appellant argues absence of proof of financial capacity.
However, once presumption under Section 139 arises, burden shifts to accused.

27. In APS Forex Services Pvt Ltd v. Shakti International Fashion Linkers, it was held that unless accused specifically disputes financial capacity and lays foundation, complainant need not initially prove source.

entities.text: APS Forex Services Pvt Ltd v. Shakti International Fashion Linkers
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 28. In present case, no effective cross-examination was conducted challenging financial capacity.
No documentary contradiction was elicited.
29. Records reveal that repeated opportunities were granted for cross-examination.
Costs were imposed.
Final opportunity was granted.
30. The accused remained absent.
Further cross- examination was closed only after sufficient indulgence.
31. Proceedings under Section 138 are summary in nature.
Section 143 mandates expeditious disposal.
32. In Indian Bank Association v. Union of India, the Hon'ble Apex Court directed day-to-day trial and strict timelines.

entities.text: Indian Bank Association v. Union of India
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 33. The accused cannot take advantage of his own negligence.
No material is produced before this Court substantiating alleged paralysis during trial stage (May 2023), particularly when cross-examination was closed in April 2023.
Illness plea remains unsubstantiated by medical records.

Srinivas vs M B Chandrakumari on 4 April, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/194172112/
7 34.
The complainant's testimony remained largely unshaken.
No material contradictions were proved.
35. Admission of borrowing Rs.3,00,000/- in reply notice strengthens existence of financial transaction.
36. The accused failed to discharge the evidentiary burden required to rebut presumption on preponderance of probabilities.
37. The Trial Court has properly analysed statutory presumptions and applied settled principles.
38. No perversity, illegality or misappreciation is demonstrated.
39. Appellate Court will not interfere with findings of fact unless findings are perverse or based on no evidence.
40. The impugned judgment is reasoned, supported by oral and documentary evidence, and consonant with statutory presumptions.
41. The sentence imposed--fine slightly exceeding cheque amount with compensation--is within statutory limits and proportionate.

42. This Court finds that the complainant successfully established issuance of cheque, dishonour,
service of notice and non-payment.
43. The statutory presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 remained unrebutted.
44. The defence of security cheque is unsupported by evidence.

45. No procedural violation causing prejudice is established.
46.
The impugned judgment is legally sustainable and does not call for interference.

Therefore,
Point No.2 to 4 are answered in Negative.
47. Point No.5:

In view of the reasons mentioned above and the findings arrived at on Point No.1 to 4, I proceed to pass the following:
ORDER

The application filed by the appellant under Section 5 of the Limitation Act,
1963, seeking condonation of delay of 371 days in preferring the present criminal appeal is hereby allowed.
The delay of 371 days in filing the appeal is condoned.

8
The Criminal Appeal filed by the appellant under Section 374(3) of Cr.P.C. is hereby dismissed.

The judgment of conviction and order of sentence dated 01.06.2023 passed in C.C.
No.16181/2020 by the XVI A.C.M.M., Bengaluru, is hereby confirmed.

The Trial Court shall take necessary steps to secure the accused to undergo sentence,
if not already complied.
Office is directed to send back the Trial Court records along with copy of this judgment forthwith.
